c.tagline: Pacific port city famed for cruise ships, Valle de Guadalupe wine country, and fresh seafood.

taxi.fareNote: Most taxis do not use meters; agree on the fare with the driver before starting the ride, especially for airport or Valle de Guadalupe trips.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's national emergency number, connecting to police, fire, and medical services.

avoid.reason: Tourist zone safe; caution in outer areas (Baja cartel presence)

hood_desc: The historic waterfront core along Boulevard Costero and Avenida López Mateos, home to the cruise terminal, the Riviera del Pacífico cultural center, and the fish market; best for first-timers who want fish tacos, souvenir shops, and cantinas all within walking distance.

The stretch of coastal hotels and restaurants south of downtown along Boulevard Costero, popular with cruise passengers and weekend visitors from California; suits travelers who want an oceanfront base close to the action without staying right downtown.

A hillside residential area above downtown known for its lookout point over the bay and marina, with a handful of boutique hotels and restaurants; good for those wanting quiet and a view over the noise of the port.

Mexico's premier wine region, about 30-40 minutes northeast of the city, dotted with boutique wineries, farm-to-table restaurants, and design-forward small hotels; suits travelers prioritizing wine tastings and countryside scenery over city sights.
A quieter stretch of sand and lagoon south of the city with family-oriented resorts and water sports; suits families and travelers wanting a beach base away from the cruise crowds.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water, as everywhere in Mexico.

transit.hours: Buses generally run about 6:00 AM to 9:00 PM; no night service, so taxis or ride apps cover late hours.
transit.pay: Cash paid to the driver on board (roughly 10-12 pesos per ride); there is no rechargeable transit card system.
transit.note: Ensenada has no metro or rail transit; local 'camiones urbanos' (urban buses) and taxis are the main public transport, with ride-hailing apps also available downtown.

bus: ABC (Autotransportes de Baja California) intercity buses to Tijuana, Mexicali, and Tecate

transit.m: ABC intercity bus toward Ensenada (transfer required)

tip.r: 10-15% at sit-down restaurants is standard and expected; not usually added automatically except for large groups.

food.name: Tacos de pescado estilo Baja
food.desc: The original battered fish taco: beer-battered white fish fried crisp, on a warm corn tortilla with cabbage, crema and salsa.

places.name: Tacos Fenix
places.note: Founded in 1970 and still one of the most traditional fish-taco stands in the city.

places.name: Mercado Negro
places.note: The old fish market; taco stands around it fry whatever came off the boats that morning.

places.name: Mariscos El Guero
places.note: Open since 1981, the locals' low-key alternative to the tourist queues.

food.name: Tostadas de mariscos
food.desc: Crisp tostadas piled with sea urchin, crab, shrimp or pismo clam and finished with one of dozens of house salsas.

places.name: La Guerrerense
places.area: Av. Lopez Mateos y Alvarado, Centro
places.note: Sabina Bandera's cart, running 60-plus years; the sea urchin tostada is the one to order.

places.name: Sabina Restaurante
places.note: The sit-down restaurant from the same family, if you want a table and a wine list.

places.name: Mariscos El Guero
places.note: Equally good tostadas without the international crowd.

food.name: Almejas gratinadas y tatemadas
food.desc: Chocolata clams from the bay either charred on the grill in their shells or baked under butter, cheese and chilli.

places.name: Mariscos Gil
places.note: No-frills stand celebrated for cheesy grilled clams and free-flowing tostadas.

places.name: Mariscos El Guero
places.note: Clams, oysters and yellowtail all straight off the local boats.

places.name: Mercado Negro
places.note: Buy clams raw at the market counters or have them grilled at the stalls behind.

food.name: Ceviche y aguachile
food.desc: Yellowtail, shrimp or scallop cured in lime, or drowned in a raw chilli-lime aguachile; Baja's answer to the heat.

places.name: Mariscos El Guero
places.note: Ceviche made from the freshest Baja yellowtail, clams, shrimp and oysters.

places.name: Mariscos Gil
places.note: Insanely fresh and cheap; the campechana comes with all-you-can-eat tostadas.

places.name: Muelle Tres
places.note: Small, much-praised seafood bar working with day-boat catch.

food.name: Ostiones frescos
food.desc: Oysters farmed in Bahia Falsa on the San Quintin and Ensenada coast, shucked to order with lime, salsa negra and saltines.

places.name: Mercado Negro
places.note: Shuckers work the counters all day; the cheapest oysters you will eat anywhere.

places.name: Muelle Tres
places.note: Oysters served raw and grilled, with a short Valle wine list.

places.name: Mariscos Gil
places.note: Reliable for a dozen on ice while you wait for the clams to char.

food.name: Cocina Baja Med
food.desc: The regional style that fuses Baja seafood with Mediterranean and Asian technique, built around Valle de Guadalupe produce.

places.name: Manzanilla
places.note: Benito Molina's restaurant, the address most credited with defining Baja Med cooking.

places.name: Muelle Tres
places.note: Casual, seasonal and consistently well reviewed by Baja food writers.

places.name: Sabina Restaurante
places.note: Refined seafood plates rooted in the same street-cart repertoire.

food.name: Vino del Valle de Guadalupe
food.desc: Mexico's wine country begins 20km inland - big nebbiolos, tempranillo blends and salty chenin blanc grown in the dry valley.

places.name: Bodegas de Santo Tomas
places.note: Mexico's oldest winery, with a tasting room and cellar tour in the middle of town.

places.name: Manzanilla
places.note: One of the strongest Valle de Guadalupe lists in the city.

places.name: Muelle Tres
places.note: Small-producer Valle wines by the glass to drink with the seafood.

food.name: Cerveza artesanal y michelada
food.desc: Baja craft beer, plus the michelada - beer over ice with lime, salsa and a chilli-salt rim, sometimes served with a shrimp on top.

places.name: Wendlandt Cerveceria
places.note: Ensenada's flagship craft brewery, driver of the whole Baja beer scene.

places.name: Agua Mala Sala de Cerveza
places.note: Local brewery taproom with a sea-themed line-up and a young crowd.

places.name: Hussong's Cantina
places.note: Open since 1892 and claimed birthplace of the margarita; noisy, sawdust-floored and essential.

landmarks: La Bufadora
One of the world's largest marine geysers, a sea cave blowhole that blasts spray 30 meters skyward from the cliffs of Punta Banda.
Valle de Guadalupe
Mexico's premier wine country just inland from the city, where more than 100 boutique wineries pour tastings amid vineyard-striped granite hills.
Riviera del Pacífico Cultural Center
A glamorous 1930s casino-hotel turned cultural center, its Spanish colonial halls, gardens and murals whispering of Hollywood's Prohibition-era escapades.
Mercado Negro (Mercado de Mariscos)
The bustling harborside fish market where vendors hawk the day's catch and neighboring stalls fry Ensenada's legendary battered fish tacos.
Ventana al Mar and the Malecón
The waterfront esplanade crowned by a colossal Mexican flag, ideal for strolling past sea lions, sculpture and Pacific sunsets.
Hussong's Cantina
Baja's oldest bar, pouring drinks since 1892 in sawdust-floored splendor and claiming bragging rights as birthplace of the margarita.
Avenida López Mateos (Calle Primera)
Ensenada's main tourist strip, a colorful parade of craft shops, taquerias, galleries and cantinas a few blocks from the cruise pier.
Bodegas de Santo Tomás
One of Mexico's oldest wineries, founded in 1888, offering barrel-room tastings in its historic downtown cellars.
Mirador El Ciprés (Chapultepec Hill)
The hillside viewpoint above town delivering sweeping panoramas of Todos Santos Bay, the harbor and the mountains beyond.
Museo Caracol (Museo de Ciencias)
A modern shell-shaped science museum on the waterfront exploring Baja California's oceans, deserts and night skies through interactive exhibits.

train.note: No passenger railway serves Ensenada or the Baja peninsula - the old Tijuana-Tecate line is freight and tourist-excursion only. Travel is by coach or car down the scenic Highway 1 from Tijuana, about 90 minutes away.

intl.to: San Diego & Los Angeles (USA) - via the Tijuana border

bus.note: ABC is the dominant Baja operator and runs from the Ensenada terminal north to Tijuana in about 90 minutes, where you connect for the San Ysidro border crossing, as well as the long haul down the peninsula to Guerrero Negro and La Paz (around 20 hours). Some services run through to San Diego and Los Angeles - you need a valid US visa and get off the bus for immigration at the border.

ferry.note: Ensenada's port is a busy cruise terminal and fishing harbour but has no scheduled passenger ferry. The Baja Ferries crossings to mainland Mexico sail from La Paz and Pichilingue, at the far southern end of the peninsula.

half.name: Tijuana
half.blurb: Mexico's busiest border city, known for Avenida Revolución nightlife, street tacos, and the modern Centro Cultural Tijuana dome.

half.name: Rosarito Beach
half.blurb: Beach town just north with a long sandy shoreline, the Foxploration film studio, and the historic Rosarito Beach Hotel.

full.name: San Quintín
full.blurb: Agricultural and fishing area south along the Pacific coast, known for oyster farms, volcanic cinder cones, and quiet beaches.
